title: Girora: Plan Trips with AI and Find People to Travel With
summary: Girora is a travel companion app that uses locally-run AI to help users plan trips, generate itineraries, and find others with similar travel interests to join their journeys, solving the fragmentation of travel planning across multiple apps.
content:
My submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 1: Touch Grass.
I built Girora, a travel companion app that helps people plan trips, share their travel plans, and find others who might want to join them.
The idea came from a simple problem: planning a trip involves a lot of small decisions. You have to choose a destination, figure out the dates and budget, plan what to do, and sometimes find people who are interested in going with you. These things can end up scattered across different apps, websites, and conversations.
I wanted to bring the main parts of this process together in one place.
Girora is built around three things: planning a trip, sharing it with others, and discovering trips to join.
Sometimes you know you want to travel, but you don't know where to start with the planning. You might have a destination in mind, a limited budget, or only a few days available.
Girora includes an AI itinerary-generation feature that helps turn travel preferences into a suggested plan. The idea is to give users a starting point instead of making them plan every detail from scratch.
For the AI part, I used Gemma 3 1B through Ollama, running locally on my computer. This gave me a way to experiment with an open-weight model and connect its generated output to the application.
Girora also lets users create trips with details such as the destination, dates, and budget.
The idea is that a trip shouldn't have to remain a private plan. Once created, it can be shared so other people can discover it and see whether it interests them.
This is the community part of the project.
Users can browse trips and express interest in joining one by sending a join request. Instead of everyone having to plan separately, Girora is intended to make it easier for people with similar travel interests to connect around a trip.
The current version demonstrates the trip discovery and join-request flows, but it doesn't yet have a shared backend. Trip data and join requests are stored

title: # I Built a .gitignore Generator Because Setting Up a Project Should Be Simpler
summary: DotGitIgnore.com is a free generator that creates technology-appropriate .gitignore files, eliminating the need to manually hunt templates or remember exclusion rules for different tech stacks and frameworks.
content:
Every developer has probably done this at some point.
You create a new project, initialize Git, and then realize you still need to create a .gitignore file.
If you're working with a familiar stack, you probably know which files and directories to exclude. But when you're starting a new project, switching technologies, or working with an unfamiliar tool, things get a little less obvious.
Should node_modules be ignored? What about build output, environment files, IDE settings, caches, or framework-specific directories?
You can write the file yourself, copy one from another project, or search GitHub for an existing template.
I wanted to make that process a little easier, so I built DotGitIgnore.com.
DotGitIgnore is a free .gitignore generator for developers.
The idea is simple: choose the technologies, languages, frameworks, or tools you're using, and generate a .gitignore file that you can use in your project.
Instead of starting from an empty file or digging through repositories to find the right template, you can put together the rules you need in one place.
You can explore the available templates and build a file suited to your project without having to remember every generated directory or temporary file for every technology you use.
It's a small tool, but it's meant to solve a real problem that comes up during everyday development.
The basic interface for a tool like this is relatively straightforward.
The more interesting challenge is the template collection behind it.
Different languages and frameworks have different conventions. Even within the same ecosystem, the files you want Git to ignore can vary depending on your workflow.
A template that works well for one project might not be enough for another. And blindly combining every possible ignore rule would make the output unnecessarily large and difficult to understand.

title: Let the LLM Talk, Let a Script Do the Math: A Three-Part Pattern for Decision Agents
summary: Architectural pattern that separates AI reasoning from deterministic computation—letting LLMs interpret user intent while local scripts handle optimization and math—improves speed, cost, and accuracy for decision-making problems like coupon matching.
content:
A quick test


You have two McDonald's coupons and can use only one:
Spend 40, get 10 off
12% off any burger
You order a ¥25 burger:
Threshold coupon: you'd have to add ¥15 more → pay ¥30
Percentage coupon: 25 × 0.88 = ¥22 → the percentage coupon wins



Now make that burger ¥40:
Threshold coupon: pay ¥30 → the threshold coupon wins

Percentage coupon: pay ¥35.2
Which coupon is cheaper depends entirely on what's in the order. There is no general answer.
That's two coupons and one item. A real order is three coupons, twenty items, plus constraints like "two people, under ¥50, keep it under 1100 kcal, at least 35g protein." The number of combinations that satisfy all of that runs into the thousands.
Ask an LLM to solve that and you get three predictable outcomes:
Slow — thousands of multiply-adds, generated token by token
Expensive — every step burns tokens
Wrong — LLM arithmetic, as anyone who's tried it knows
So this project started from one rule:
The LLM handles understanding and expression. A script handles computation and determinism.
User speaks plainly
   │  "two people, under ¥50, nothing too greasy"
   ▼
LLM (WorkBuddy) parses intent ──► hard constraints
   │  max_payable=45, max_calories=1100, min_protein=35
   ▼
McDonald's MCP fetches real data ──► store menu / nutrition / coupons
   │
   ▼
optimize_meal.py (local, no network) ──► enumerate + best-coupon match
   │
   ▼
LLM turns results back into plain language ──► three plans




Role
Owns
Doesn't own




LLM
Interpreting "nothing too greasy"; narrating results
Money math, calorie math, remembering menus


MCP
Structured, trustworthy data
Decisions


Local script
Enumeration, filtering, coupon matching, ranking
Natural language



The payoff is direct: the script runs in milliseconds, is reproducible, costs zero tokens, and never gets the money wrong.

title: I’m 19, a former game dev, and now working in pentesting.
summary: A 19-year-old shares their career transition from game development to penetration testing, driven by curiosity about web infrastructure and security, demonstrating that entry into cybersecurity is achievable through self-study and hands-on projects.
content:
Hey DEV! I’m 19, a former game dev, and now working in pentesting. 👋


Hey everyone, 
I'm 19 years old and currently working full-time as a penetration tester. I've been lurking around the DEV community for a while now, and I figured it's finally time to break the ice and make my first post. 
Honestly, if you told me a few years ago that this is what I’d be doing for a living today, I wouldn't have believed you.
My tech journey actually started out in game development. I loved building things from scratch, but eventually, I got super curious about how the web and data infrastructure actually worked under the hood. 
That curiosity pulled me down a massive rabbit hole of web dev and networking, which quickly collided head-on with cybersecurity. I realized I liked networks and web apps a lot, but I fell completely in love with the security side of things:
Finding vulnerabilities (and figuring out how to exploit them safely)
Understanding how systems break
Learning how to properly patch and fix them
I spent a ton of my time self-studying, grinding through labs, and building personal projects until I managed to land my current role. 
I’m here because I want to start documenting my journey, sharing some of my findings (the non-confidential ones, of course!), and learning from the rest of you. 
If you’re into cybersec, networking, web dev, or just tech in general, drop a comment and say hi! I'd love to connect and hear what projects everyone else is working on right now.
Cheers! 🍻

title: RethinkDB at 1,419 Matches and Nothing on 28015: When the Driver Port Is the Right Question
summary: Analysis using ZoomEye search data illustrates how product counts and port scans reveal different aspects of RethinkDB deployment exposure, demonstrating that port-level queries show whether services are published to the internet.
content:
RethinkDB at 1,419 Matches and Nothing on 28015: When the Driver Port Is the Right Question


A measurement that returns zero is often the most informative result in a set, provided the query behind it was the right one. The RethinkDB pair shows both halves of that statement.
Both queries ran on 2026-10-02 in the all-types scope.
app="RethinkDB", returned 1,419 matches.
https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=YXBwPSJSZXRoaW5rREIi
port=28015, returned zero matches.
https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=cG9ydD0yODAxNQ%3D%3D
A zero is a claim about the world, and it is only as strong as the query. A query for a port with no other condition is a weak instrument: it counts whatever happened to answer on that port and be recorded, and it says nothing about which software is listening.
A web administration console is a different interface with different rules. It presents a UI, it is frequently placed behind a proxy, and it exposes a JSON endpoint alongside the pages.
The first question is which addresses the cluster interfaces are bound to. A cluster that binds its driver, its intra-cluster port and its console to private interfaces has no external exposure regardless of the software's own authentication behaviour.
The pair illustrates a general point about exposure measurement. A product count answers whether something is installed. A port count answers whether a particular interface is published. Neither answers whether the interface is reachable to an authenticated user, and the zero here is only meaningful because the port in question is one that sensible deployments do not publish.
[1] ZoomEye search, app="RethinkDB", executed 2026-10-02 UTC, exact total 1,419. https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=YXBwPSJSZXRoaW5rREIi

[2] ZoomEye search, port=28015, executed 2026-10-02 UTC, exact total 0. https://www.zoomeye.ai/searchResult?q=cG9ydD0yODAxNQ%3D%3D

[3] RethinkDB project home page. https://rethinkdb.com/

title: From Mobile Tap to Autonomous Agent: A Reference Architecture for the AI-Native FinTech Stack
summary: Reference architecture for AI-native fintech systems shows how autonomous agents can interpret ambiguous customer instructions while delegating actual financial execution to deterministic, auditable contracts that enforce authorization boundaries.
content:
AI-native FinTech changes more than the user interface.
It changes how we need to think about authority, execution, and financial truth.
A traditional payment flow is relatively straightforward:
User
  ↓
Mobile App
  ↓
API
  ↓
Financial Service
  ↓
Payment Rail

Introduce an autonomous agent and another decision-making layer appears:
Customer Intent
      ↓
Agent Reasoning
      ↓
Policy / Authorization
      ↓
Financial Services
      ↓
Payment Rail

The important architectural question is no longer only:
Who authenticated?
It also becomes:
What exactly is software acting on behalf of that customer allowed to do?
An AI agent can interpret ambiguous instructions, gather information, choose tools, retry operations, and coordinate multiple services.
That flexibility is useful.
But financial systems cannot allow probabilistic reasoning to become the final source of authority.
Consider a customer instruction:
Pay my broadband bill every month if it stays below ₹1,500.
This is not a direct payment command.
It contains several constraints that first need to become structured financial intent:
{
  "intentType": "PAY_BILL",
  "billerId": "ISP_291",
  "maximumAmountMinor": 150000,
  "currency": "INR"
}

The agent can help interpret the instruction.
But the payment system should execute the structured contract—not the original natural-language sentence.
That boundary creates a useful architectural rule:
Reasoning may be probabilistic. Financial execution should remain deterministic.
A customer may successfully authenticate, but that does not mean an agent should automatically receive every permission available to the customer.
Instead of handing the agent broad account authority, the platform can create a bounded delegation:
action: PAY_BILL
biller: ISP_291
maxAmount: 150000
expiresAt: ...

The exact implementation might use scopes, server-side grants, capability tokens, mandates, or another authorization model.
The principle is the same:
Give the agent only the authority req

title: I Shipped 8 Free AI Writing Tools With Zero Budget — Here's What I Learned
summary: Developer built eight free writing tools with zero API costs by using deterministic algorithms instead of LLMs, removing signup barriers, and processing text client-side for privacy, finding 90% of real usage doesn't require neural networks.
content:
People keep asking me how much I'm paying in API bills. The answer is zero. Not "free tier" zero — actually zero.
Earlier this year I launched HumanWritr (https://humanwritr.com/), eight writing tools: a text humanizer, paraphraser, grammar checker, AI detector, plagiarism checker, word counter, AI SEO content writer, and an AI image detector. No funding, no team, no LLM API. Just me, a Cloudflare Worker, and an unreasonable amount of coffee.
Here's what I figured out along the way.
This was the big realization. Everyone assumes "AI writing tool" means piping everything through GPT. But think about what users actually do: fix grammar, reword a paragraph, count words, check if text looks AI-generated.
A paraphraser with a serious synonym database handles rewording fine. Grammar rules catch grammar errors — that's literally what they're for. An AI detector looking at linguistic markers (sentence uniformity, predictable word choices) does the job without a neural network. These deterministic approaches are instant, they cost nothing per request, and they work offline.
Sure, they won't write you a novel. But 90% of real usage isn't "write me a novel." It's "fix this paragraph."
I didn't plan this as a feature. Running everything client-side was originally just a cost decision — no servers processing text means no server bills. But then users started mentioning it in feedback: they liked that their drafts never left their browser.
Think about it — people paste cover letters, business plans, personal essays into these tools. "We don't see your text because we can't see your text" is a stronger privacy promise than any policy page. Architecture as a feature. I'll take it.
Every signup form is a tiny rejection. "Give me your email before I'll help you." I removed the requirement completely — every tool works the second the page loads. There's a login if you want it. Nothing needs it.
I can't give you exact numbers, but the difference in usage before and after was not subtle
